preamble.text: Historical snapshot: later evidence may be reflected in current research pages and corrections.
Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. GPT-6 Astra reaches OpenAI's Critical cyber tier while external ARC-AGI-3 testing exposes a large provider-state-management effect

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: B · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 9/10 (Paradigm-level) Importance rationale: Paradigm-level if the central capability claims survive independent, contamination-resistant evaluation: a broadly deployed system that genuinely approaches saturation on ARC-AGI-3 and FrontierMath Tier 4 while showing frontier computer-use and Critical cyber capability would force major reassessment of what present AI systems can do. The score measures consequence if true, not confidence. It was explicitly reviewed from 8 to 9 after the September 3 release and external ARC Prize results. The 99.9% ARC headline is strongly harness-dependent—62.7% under the provider-neutral Standard harness—while FrontierMath and the strongest cyber results remain substantially first-party, so importance does not erase attribution/provenance uncertainty.

Demonstrated: Astra is now an externally available released model surface rather than only a forthcoming model. ARC Prize independently verifies 62.7% ARC-AGI-3 Semi-Private at max reasoning under Standard and 99.9% at high reasoning under Provider Adapter. ARC Prize reports the Provider Adapter was approximately 3.66x faster by aggregate recorded elapsed time and used 49% fewer total tokens across 167 game-reasoning pairs solved by both harnesses. OpenAI's public API documentation lists a 1,050,000-token context window and 128,000 max output tokens.

Claimed: OpenAI reports 100% ExploitBench, 97.6% FrontierMath Tier 4 v2, 57.9% Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 72.6% OSWorld 2.0 at roughly 40 minutes/task versus 65.7% at roughly 75 minutes for GPT-5.6 Sol in its latency simulation. OpenAI continues to report autonomous zero-day discovery/exploit chaining under specialized cyber access and classifies Astra at its Critical cybersecurity threshold.

Mechanism: OpenAI does not disclose architecture or parameter count sufficient for causal architectural attribution. The observed system combines the Astra weights with reasoning effort, tools, long context, model-specific persistent reasoning state and compaction. OpenAI attributes alignment gains to changes spanning pre-training data through reinforcement-learning grading and adds system-level monitoring/safeguards. ARC Prize's Provider Adapter specifically preserves opaque reasoning state across requests and compacts long interactions, unlike its Standard harness where the model must choose visible notes to carry forward.

Strongest baseline: For long-horizon abstract reasoning, the strongest attribution control is Astra against itself under ARC Prize Standard versus Provider Adapter. For model-generation comparison, GPT-5.6 Sol is OpenAI's main baseline. For FrontierMath, Epoch's benchmark methodology/provenance is the key external context, but an independent Epoch-run Astra score was not recovered in this activation.

Regime: Released model with limited/rolling availability. ARC Prize provides independent harness-controlled evaluation. OpenAI capability, cyber and safety measurements remain largely first-party and some use research/internal harnesses that may differ from production surfaces.

Limitations: The central cyber capability measurements remain OpenAI-run and have not been independently reproduced.; ARC-AGI-3 varies from 62.7% to 99.9% depending on harness/state management, so the 99.9% number is not a provider-neutral raw-model score.; ARC Prize calls the result a major milestone but explicitly does not treat ARC-AGI-3 saturation as proof of AGI.; OpenAI's 97.6% FrontierMath Tier 4 v2 is not independently reproduced in the evidence recovered here; Epoch discloses OpenAI funding and exclusive benchmark access to a subset.; The internal 20-vulnerability cyber benchmark and hardened-browser/OS assessments are not public enough to replay.; The 56%-versus-0 honeypot result from the earlier report is a specific simulated evaluation without production cyber safeguards, not a real-world misalignment rate.; OpenAI reports decreased chain-of-thought monitorability relative to GPT-5.6 Sol under adversarial instructions even while broader alignment results improve.; Provider Adapter's opaque reasoning state is not exposed to independent semantic inspection, so exactly which retained information causes the ARC jump is unresolved.; Irregular’s external evaluation was conducted with OpenAI and reports no successful attacks on fully hardened targets or Elite challenges; it does not independently reproduce OpenAI’s separate hardened-browser/operating-system chains or adjudicate the Critical designation.

Contrary evidence: The provider-neutral ARC Prize Standard harness score of 62.7% is far below OpenAI's 99.9% launch headline and prevents treating the latter as harness-independent capability.; Astra's stronger overall alignment coexists with weaker chain-of-thought monitorability in adversarial settings; better behavioral control does not imply easier internal auditing.; The strongest cyber results require specialized tools/access and therefore do not establish equivalent capability in default production deployment.; FrontierMath provenance/access creates a nontrivial independence concern for interpreting near-saturation without an external run.

Open evidence gaps: Irregular has published an external evaluation conducted with OpenAI, but this is not an independent reproduction of OpenAI’s distinct browser-compromise/operating-system exploit chains or an independent determination that Astra meets OpenAI’s Critical threshold.; The causal source of the 62.7%→99.9% ARC-AGI-3 gap is not decomposed beyond Provider Adapter preserving opaque reasoning state and compaction.; OpenAI's FrontierMath Tier 4 v2 result lacks an independent Epoch-run Astra entry in the recovered evidence.; The contribution of alignment training, monitoring, classifiers and deterministic system gates to reduced unauthorized behavior remains unresolved.

Sources: https://openai.com/index/path-to-astra/ · https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ · https://openai.com/index/safety-overview-gpt-6-astra/ · https://arcprize.org/blog/astra · https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/frontiermath-tier-4-v2 · https://irregular.cv/research/assessing-gpt-6-astra
2. China proposes new technology export catalog entries and interim registration for AI exports

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If implemented as proposed and applied to covered transfers, export controls and pre-export registration across frontier AI, compute and information-processing technologies could alter cross-border technology transfer, research collaboration and global capability diffusion. The consequence is major, while the exact scope remains bounded by the official annex, public-domain exceptions and streamlined pathways; this is a proposal with an interim registration mechanism, not proof of an adopted permanent catalog amendment or changed export outcomes.

What changed: On 2026-10-16, China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology issued Announcement No. 48, proposing changes to the technology export catalog and opening consultation through 2026-11-15. The proposal covers 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics, including 23 AI-related entries described as involving large models, agents, computing clusters and information processing. The announcement also states that pre-export registration applies from publication until the formal catalog revision takes effect for technologies listed in its annexes, with specified accelerated pathways and a stated exclusion for AI technologies already in the public domain through open source or academic publication. This is a proposal plus interim registration measure; the detailed WPS annexes were not decoded, and adoption, case-level scope and export outcomes remain unverified. Why it matters: If implemented as proposed, the measure could affect cross-border transfer, licensing and collaboration involving covered AI, computing and other technologies. Its practical reach depends on exact annex definitions, public-domain and facilitation provisions, and the eventual final catalog; it does not establish a blanket ban on AI exports.

Demonstrated: The official notice and FAQ document publication and the announced policy text; they do not establish final adoption of the proposed permanent catalog changes or measurable enforcement effects.

Claimed: The official notice proposes additions to the Chinese technology export catalog and sets an interim pre-export registration process for the listed technologies until a formal revision takes effect.

Mechanism: Consultation on proposed catalog additions plus temporary registration before export of technologies in the notice's attachments; the notice describes specific licensing facilitation and public-domain provisions.
Strongest baseline: The existing technology export catalog and the formal amended catalog once published.
Regime: China's technology export management; proposal covers AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics, with 23 proposed AI entries and a stated interim measure pending formal catalog revision.

Limitations: The catalog revision is proposed and was open for consultation through 2026-11-15 at the time of this review; it is not yet a final amended catalog.; The announcement supplies detailed technical scope in WPS attachments that were not decoded in this review; this account cannot determine whether a specific technology or transaction is covered.; The measure is described as interim pre-export registration until the amended catalog takes effect. No registration, enforcement, denial or export-impact data were reviewed.; The stated public-domain exclusion and specified automatic or expedited licensing provisions narrow or qualify the proposed controls; this is not evidence of a general AI export ban.; This review is an evidence summary, not a case-specific legal determination.

Open evidence gaps: The official announcement's WPS Annex 1 contains the proposed control points and technical indicators, including detailed AI categories; these were not inspected.; No final catalog amendment, transition notice, implementation record, or public data about registrations and enforcement was inspected.
Sources: https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/zcfb/dwmygl/art/2026/art_61446ab4beee4f63973d4d0ab3097648.html · https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/xwfb/xwfyrth/art/2026/art_d7661dbf62794345a221404f82a25959.html
compute_hardware

items: Agentic high-level synthesis with RTL refinement reports faster FPGA kernels than direct RTL on a bounded benchmark — importance 4/10 · The authors compare agents designing FPGA kernels directly in RTL with workflows that use high-level synthesis (HLS) and post-HLS RTL refinement. On an 11-task benchmark, they report a 2.62× geometric-mean speedup in simulated execution time for agent-based HLS with RTL refinement over direct RTL across 13 valid task/model pairs; agent-based HLS alone reports 2.31× across 15 valid pairs. The experiments use Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.6 Sol in the same pi harness, AMD Alveo U55C and Vitis 2025.2, with each experiment run once. The metric combines simulated cycle count with the greater of post-route clock period or target period. These are paper-reported FPGA results, not an independent reproduction, production ASIC benchmark or measured cost reduction. — FCMO-727579227CA4

blocks.text: evaluation_science

items: GPT-6 Astra reaches OpenAI's Critical cyber tier while external ARC-AGI-3 testing exposes a large provider-state-management effect — importance 9/10 · OpenAI designated GPT-6 Astra its first Critical cybersecurity-capability model under its Preparedness Framework, reporting internal exploit-benchmark and expert assessments. Irregular’s separate public evaluation, conducted with OpenAI, reports Astra solved 86/226 FrontierCyber challenges versus 34/226 for GPT-5.6 Sol, achieved 59% versus 27% average CyScenarioBench success, and solved 20/22 Atomic Challenges. Irregular also reports that neither model solved an Elite challenge or successfully attacked a fully hardened target. These external results support a substantial capability increase in bounded test settings, while not independently reproducing OpenAI’s separate browser/OS chains or validating OpenAI’s Critical-tier decision. ARC Prize separately reports a large ARC-AGI-3 score difference between its Standard and Provider Adapter harnesses, which preserve different kinds of state. — FCMO-841949AEA161

Set-level reinforcement learning improves judged quality and diversity of scientific idea portfolios — importance 5/10 · The Oct 15 arXiv preprint introduces a set-level reinforcement-learning objective that scores each idea by its judged quality and semantic distance from earlier ideas in the same generated set. The authors train Qwen3-8B and report a Creative Utility score of 0.64 for the no-thinking variant and 0.51 for the thinking variant on a 1,740-instance, contamination-free test set built from 2026 papers; the reported baselines are 0.38 for Claude Opus 4.8 and 0.28 for GPT-6 Astra. A four-expert pilot across 60 instances reports similar counts of promising ideas to Claude and slightly more unique ideas, while a coding-agent proof-of-concept on 15 instances reports comparable success@k. These are author-reported results using model-based evaluation; the author-linked code repository currently says code, data and models are forthcoming. — FCMO-E39389D9B9E5

blocks.text: multimodality_world_models

items: Coda reallocates flow-matching VLA inference compute to a learned endpoint correction — importance 4/10 · The authors introduce Coda, a learned endpoint correction for frozen flow-matching vision-language-action policies. On RoboTwin 2.0 simulation, they report that five-step Coda raises task success from 71.64% to 74.68% over a matched five-step baseline across 50 Easy tasks, while reducing measured model-forward latency 30.2% against the default ten-step policy. A separate 13-task comparison reports a 5.69-point success gain at nearly equal latency, and an implementation on frozen SmolVLA reports a two-step gain from 60.8% to 69.4%. The paper reports no clear average gain on its visual-randomization Hard protocol; latency excludes communication and physical execution, and no real-robot evaluation or independent reproduction was conducted. — FCMO-172E4E20E2DE

blocks.text: labs_industry

items: A 41-country paper reports a shift toward senior workers at AI-adopting multinationals — importance 7/10 · A Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper dated September 21, 2026 analyzes 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records across 41 countries, inferring AI adoption from job advertisements mentioning generative AI. In an instrumented event study of foreign multinational affiliates, the authors report that by March 2026 the junior share was 1.9 percentage points below matched controls. Senior employment was 6.7% higher; the 2.5% lower junior-employment estimate was not statistically significant, and total employment was 3.3% higher at marginal significance. The paper’s model-based decomposition suggests modest seniority-biased productivity gains. These are author-reported estimates, not independent replication or a representative global labor census. The paper identifies platform coverage, job-ad-based adoption timing, and an untestable instrument exclusion restriction as limits; results concern digitally attached multinational affiliates. This differs in population and method from Anthropic’s internal workforce report and is comparative evidence, not replication. — FCMO-D47DE43C40AB

Brazil opens consultation on AI ethics guidance for human-subject research — importance 4/10 · On 15 October 2026, Brazil’s Ministry of Health opened a public consultation, scheduled through 31 March 2027, on three INAEP documents for ethical review of AI use in research with human participants: a guidance document, the MARIAH risk-assessment matrix, and a reference notebook. The Portuguese materials cover health and human/social-science research and recommend context-sensitive, proportionate review; MARIAH supports human committee deliberation and does not automatically approve or reject studies. The package is under consultation, not evidence of binding adoption or changed research practice. — FCMO-B22B34481FEB

CCTV reports release of China’s Qiusuo 4.0 AI evaluation framework with 16 tools — importance 4/10 · The Digital China Summit website, citing CCTV News, reported that China’s Qiusuo 4.0 AI evaluation benchmark was released on October 13, 2026. The report describes a national-standard framework with 16 assessment tools across compute, models and intelligent systems, safety, and industry applications, and says lighter code tools for compute, large models, and agents are open source. It also reports pilots and product validation in finance, power, and petrochemicals based on a quotation from a China Electronics Standardization Institute official. The source page does not provide the issuing institute’s release, benchmark specifications, code, or pilot records; scope and implementation claims therefore remain attributed and unverified. — FCMO-E6C1CA1DDF8D

blocks.text: training_data

items: CodeMidas builds coding RL tasks from source code and reports gains on five external benchmarks — importance 5/10 · The authors introduce CodeMidas, a pipeline that derives executable reinforcement-learning tasks from implemented functionality in open-source codebases, constructs execution-grounded tests, and filters environments using execution checks and solution rollouts. They report 5,545 training tasks from 3,185 repositories across 23 languages and 15 technical domains. Training MiMo-V2.5 with GRPO on this dataset reportedly improves all five listed external coding benchmarks relative to the same initial policy and evaluation settings. Examples include DeepSWE pass rate rising from 10.0% to 21.7%, Terminal-Bench v2.1 from 63.7% to 72.2%, and ProgramBench Almost Solved from 4.5 to 21.5. The authors report task-set disjointness from CodeMidas Val and the five external benchmark sets. These are author-reported results for one model/training setup, not an independent reproduction or general scaling law. — FCMO-79D9ABD90F7D
